newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN ELECTRABEL SEEN LOSING ITS SPARK.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN ELECTRABEL SEEN LOSING ITS SPARK.

text.p: Belgian electricity utility Electrabel is expected on Monday to report slightly improved annual profits for 1996, but with more competition on the way analysts are downgrading the share to hold.
Estimates for the rise in net profit varied between four and five percent from the 28.8 billion Belgian francs generated in 1995.
"My figure for 1996 is 29.6 billion francs," BBL analyst Guenter Klaffke said. "That is about four percent up and the same as I expect the net dividend to increase."
"I rate the share a weak hold for the moment," he added.
Analyst Sandra Vandersmissen at G-Securities was slightly more optimistic on the results but had a similar view on the share.
"I expect group net profit in 1996 to be 30.26 billion francs," she said. That is a rise of five percent.
"We had rated the share as a buy, but will change it to a hold," she added.
Both analysts predicted the net share dividend would rise four percent to 352 francs from 339 in 1995.
"Electrabel has raised its dividend by four percent a year for years. It will continue to do so," Klaffke said.
Vandersmissen calculated 1996 earnings per share at 547 francs, slightly below the consensus estimate of 549 on Reuters Securities 3000.

The analysts noted that although Electrabel was well placed to face the increasing competition that should accompany the progressive liberalisation of the European energy supply markets, it would nevertheless weigh on future performance.

They noted the long-term domestic electricity supply deals the firm -- which has a virtual monopoly in Belgian -- has been negotiating with local communes that should guarantee regular income for years to come.
The European Commission has challenged these deal which have a life-span of up to 30 years, but the analysts said they felt sure a compromise would be struck at about 10 years or so.
"That is still a long time, so there is no real threat from that quarter," BBL's Klaffke said.

A greater threat is posed in the industrial sector, which is due to be fully open to international competition in 2000, and where French and Dutch generators are known to be eyeing their opportunities.
But even there the threat is seen as limited.
"Maybe along the borders; nowhere else," Vandersmissen said.
"As long as there is no dumping, Electrabel will not suffer much," Klaffke said.
"But overall the liberalisation will be negative for Electrabel," he added.
He added that he also expected the 1996 bottom line to be dented by higher taxation.
"The Belgian government needs the money. It wants to meet the Maastricht treaty criteria," Klaffke said.
At 1015 GMT on Thursday Electrabel shares were down 50 francs at 8,120 francs.
Electrabel is controlled by Belgium's Tractebel via its Powerfin unit.
